title: Runtime guardrails: throughput, fallbacks, and isolation review
next_steps: Run 2-hour baseline throughput benchmark on Dedicated pool (Jared + Beacon infra) - target window 2025-11-12
Share security pack (SOC2 cert, SSO/SAML integration guide, KMS options) - Alyssa - 2025-11-07
Provide cost sheet for 3-month reserved Dedicated capacity and hosted fallback pricing - Alyssa - 2025-11-08
Schedule 30-min pilot kickoff to onboard VPC peering and test KV cache behaviour - Toni + Sam - 2025-11-13
action_items: Alyssa Park - send security pack and pricing - due 2025-11-07
Jared Kim - prepare benchmark script and sample payloads for 100k RPS token mix - due 2025-11-10
Sam Lee - open firewall ports for VPC peering and provide bastion access creds - due 2025-11-11
Lena Wu - list compliance questions and share SOC2 scope - due 2025-11-09
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-05 15:00 UTC | Duration ~52m
Attendees: Alyssa Park (Redwood AE), Jared Kim (Redwood SE), Toni Alvarez (Redwood SE), Maya Sharma (Beacon Infra Lead), Carlos Diaz (CTO), Sam Lee (Platform Engineer), Lena Wu (Security), Speaker 6 (maybe recording glitch)

Summary: Mid-deep dive on Dedicated vs hosted runtime tradeoffs, guardrails for noisy-tenant isolation, KV / prefix cache behavior for short chat-ish workloads, batching/quantization effects on tail latency, and VPC/on-prem connectivity implications. Customer wants throughput guarantees for peak hours and safe fallbacks with minimal cost/regression risk.

Topics covered: Dedicated pool sizing, capacity fencing, autoscale vs reserved, fallback routing to hosted, KV cache TTL and cold-starts, prefix vs full KV policies, continuous batching tradeoffs, quantization (4-bit vs 8-bit), SSO/KMS, audit logs, and pilot plan.

[00:00] Alyssa: Okay everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then we'll get into Jared's perf notes. Maya, do you want to quickly state success criteria?
[00:12] Maya: Yeah, sure. For Beacon the top line is: during peak clinic hours we need a 99.9% token latency under 300 ms for median and 95th below 550 ms, and cost per 1k tokens needs to stay under the cap we discussed in the RFI. We also need data never to leave our VPC for PHI.
[00:30] Carlos: adding to that, we want predictable behaviour — no surprise noisy tenant spikes. If we need reserved capacity so be it, but we want fallback paths that don't kill UX.
[00:45] Alyssa: Great. Jared, take it away on runtime guardrails.
[00:51] Jared: Cool. First, quick recap of the runtime internals relevant to this: our serving runtime uses continuous batching and a KV-prefix cache keyed by prompt hash plus session id. So two levers: batching window and cache TTL. If you push batching too hard you can get better throughput but higher tail latency. For Dedicated we can carve isolated GPU pools with capacity fencing so noisy tenants can't preempt your slot — that's the main isolation lever.
[01:25] Sam: quick q — how deterministic is the prefix cache on restart? Like if a pod cycles mid-day do we lose the hot prefixes and cause a cold-surge?
[01:35] Jared: Good call. With Dedicated we recommend warm-up policies: a rolling restart with pinned cache warmers, or persistent cache nodes when you choose persistent KV. For hosted fallback the prefix cache is regional and cold-starts can spike, we account for that in our fallback SLOs. There's also hybrid: local on-GPU KV for hot prefixes plus regional backing store.
[02:05] Lena: for PHI we need to understand key ownership — does Redwood hold keys if we use Hosted fallback?
[02:15] Alyssa: We support customer KMS for Dedicated and Private. For hosted we can integrate customer-managed keys via our KMS proxy — there are a few caveats for backups. We'll send the security pack with exact KMS flow diagrams.
[02:30] Maya: okay good.

[03:00] Jared: Let's talk numbers observed on a 70B model baseline: in hosted, with default batching window (15 ms) and no prefix caching, median token latency ~110 ms, 95th ~420 ms under steady load; under bursty cold-start patterns 95th can hit 780 ms. In Dedicated with fenced capacity and tuned batching (8 ms) plus hot-prefix on-GPU cache we see median ~85 ms, 95th ~320 ms, and much smaller variability. Quantization to Q4_0 (4-bit) reduced cost ~40% with a small median latency improvement, but 95th tail regressed slightly unless kernels are tuned — that's where our kernel selector matters.
[03:50] Carlos: are those hosted numbers multi-tenant noisy effects or single-tenant baselines?
[03:55] Jared: The hosted figures are from our multi-tenant cluster with quota isolation; they include occasional noisy bursts. The dedicated numbers are from reserved pools with capacity-fencing, single-tenant-like behaviour.

[04:30] Maya: can you explain fallback routing? If Dedicated is saturated, what happens — drop, queue, or redirect to hosted?
[04:40] Toni: We support policy-based routing: you can configure hard SLOs to prefer Dedicated and set traffic overflow to hosted with throttles and token-level cost controls. Mechanically, requests route to Redwood's control-plane policy which will check Dedicated capacity; if below threshold it mirrors or routes to hosted model variant with same model family (we recommend a smaller quantized variant for fallback).
[05:05] Sam: Mirror — meaning you send to both and take first response? That could double token cost...
[05:12] Toni: Mirror is optional, used for A/B safety checks during rollout. For production fallback you usually route to hosted synchronously or return a degraded answer if latency critical. You can also return a semantic degradation prompt telling user the model is in reduced mode.

[05:40] Lena: audit logs? We need tamper-evident logs for decisions and SSO traces.
[05:46] Alyssa: Yes, we emit per-request tracing, decision logs for routing, and integrate with your SIEM via a pushed syslog or S3 sink. We'll include file paths and retention options in the security pack.

[06:10] Speaker 6: (audio glitch) ...sorry lost last bit.

[06:25] Jared: On batching vs latency tradeoff: continuous batching aggregates requests for X ms or until GPU is full. For short-turn chatty workloads (like Beacon's typical 20-60 token responses) batching beyond 12 ms starts hurting P95. We recommend dynamic batching that adapts to observed inter-arrival distributions; Dedicated gives more control — you can be conservative on the batching window and still maintain throughput because your GPUs aren't stolen.
[07:00] Maya: what about KV eviction policies? If we keep too many sessions hot the GPU memory becomes constrained.
[07:10] Jared: We support LRU with TTL, and also a pin-list API to keep specific conversation prefixes pinned. For Beacon we'd suggest TTL ~30 min for active clinic sessions and a pin for top 1% VIP sessions. We can expose metrics so you see eviction rates and hit ratios.

[07:45] Carlos: quantization — we have regulatory concerns about determinism. Does quantization cause reproducibility issues in outputs?
[07:55] Jared: Slight nondeterminism can appear with aggressive quant, especially with int8 kernels and per-token sampling randomness, but we treat quant as a performance/compression knob; we recommend running your eval prompts against quant variants to measure regressions. Redwood Optimize can run the evaluation harness and flag regressions per prompt set.

[08:30] Sam: For the Dedicated pool sizing — do you have a rule-of-thumb for tokens-per-GPU for our mix? We run 70% short completions ~30 tokens, 30% multi-turn longer ~200 tokens.
[08:42] Jared: Empirically, for that mix on A100-like hardware with fp16, one GPU ~100k tokens/min sustained. But real answer depends on batching efficiency and KV hit-rate. With on-GPU KV and optimized batching you can push that up by ~25%. We'll bench with your exact payloads.

[09:10] Maya: and noisy tenant isolation — what happens if another Redwood customer floods shared infra in hosted mode?
[09:18] Toni: hosted has quota and soft rate limits; we detect noisy patterns and throttle at tenant-level. But isolation is probabilistic in multi-tenant infra — that's the difference vs Dedicated. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated with capacity fencing.

[09:45] Lena: If we do Dedicated but want cost savings, can we autoscale down at night and still guarantee morning peaks?
[09:53] Jared: Yes, but we advise a hybrid: maintain a base reserved capacity sufficient for warm caches and expected morning spikes; autoscale for burst. Cold cache on scale-up will hurt early requests — we mitigate with pre-warm scripts and prefetching top prefixes.

[10:25] Carlos: are prefetch and warmers supported out-of-the-box or require engineering?
[10:30] Jared: We provide both: a warm-up SDK + example scripts and a managed warmers feature for Dedicated customers. The managed warmers can be scheduled to run before known windows.

[11:00] Sam: question on on-prem — we may eventually want a private deployment. How different is the runtime there, and are the kernels the same?
[11:08] Jared: On-prem uses the same runtime binary with hardware abstraction layer differences; kernel selection is consistent but you'll need to provide GPU drivers and potentially tune for your chip. Private deployments support full data-plane control and the same API surface. The big work is networking and ops — we've got an on-prem playbook.

[11:40] Maya: we also have strict egress rules. VPC peering seems doable?
[11:46] Toni: yes, we offer VPC peering and private-link style connectors. For Private (air-gapped) we can ship a bundle. For Hosted+Dedic we can do VPC peering plus customer KMS so data keys never leave your KMS. We'll include the network diagram in the security pack.

[12:10] Jared: Back to the kernel selection and quantization notes — we recommend starting with a Q8 (8-bit) variant for fallback hosted routes because it tends to be more stable for 95th. Q4 gives better cost but requires per-model kernel tuning.

[12:40] Carlos: curious about measuring noisy influence: do you provide per-request token-level cost and latency breakdown?
[12:48] Alyssa: Yes, Console shows token-level breakdown, per-model latency histograms, and you can filter by route, API key, and prefix. We can provide a sample dashboard export showing your traffic slice.

[13:20] Maya: what about failover correctness — do we see semantic differences between model variants used as fallback? We can't give clinicians wrong diagnoses.
[13:28] Jared: That risk exists. Two mitigations: 1) fallback to same family but quantized model version that has been validated on your eval set; 2) route to a safety policy that flags responses to human queue if confidence is low. We recommend conservative fallbacks and an eval suite for clinical prompts.

[14:00] Speaker 6: (inaudible)

[14:10] Toni: Example config we propose: Reserved Dedicated base = 8 GPUs (warm cache), burst pool autoscale to 12 GPUs, overflow to hosted Q8 variant with hard throttle at 30% traffic, and rollout mirroring during pilot only. That keeps 95th under target while bounding cost.

[14:35] Carlos: can we simulate cost and latency under a follow-up run?
[14:40] Alyssa: yes — Jared will provide a benchmark harness. We'll need sample payloads and peak hour traces.

[15:00] Jared: I'll describe the benchmark harness: it's a replay tool that preserves inter-arrival time distribution, uses real prompt/payload size histogram, and supports toggling cache hit-rates and warmers. It reports median/P95/P99 for token latency, GPU utilization, and KV hit ratios. Expect 1-2 hours to run a representative run.

[15:35] Sam: what about KV consistency under replication — if a node dies mid-session do we block?
[15:42] Jared: We use eventual consistent regional backing with fast local fallback to regional store: if local on-GPU KV misses, we check the regional store — that adds ~50-120 ms. With Dedicated persistent KV you can get <10 ms local hits. We'll show the replication topology in the docs.

[16:10] Maya: can we pin certain conversation IDs to a specific node to avoid replication impact? That sounds risky for ops but may reduce latency variance.
[16:20] Jared: We provide a pin API, but recommend it only for VIP sessions due to single-point-of-failure risk; instead prefer replication and warmers.

[16:45] Carlos: what telemetry will we get during pilot? We need P50/P95/P99, eviction rates, kernel conf, quantization variant, and routing logs.
[16:55] Alyssa: we'll export per-request traces, plus a pilot dashboard template.

[17:15] Lena: security question — if we do Hosted fallback, how do we prevent logs that contain PHI from being stored?
[17:24] Toni: we can scrub or redact PHI on ingest with user-provided redaction rules before it reaches hosted storage, or route sensitive traffic always to Dedicated/Private. We'll include our redaction options and retention controls in the security pack.

[17:50] Jared: Note on kernel selection again: for some model architectures the optimized int8 kernels give order-of-magnitude throughput improvement but require a small calibration run on representative prompts. We can run calibration in the pilot.

[18:20] Maya: timeline question: we want to be live for a beta cohort mid-December. Is that feasible?
[18:27] Alyssa: yes — with a 3-week pilot and 2 weeks for hardening we can aim for limited beta mid-Dec, assuming approvals. We'll map tasks after this call.

[18:45] Carlos: procurement / contracts — any minimums on Dedicated?
[18:50] Alyssa: Dedicated minimums are modest for pilot — e.g., 8 GPU minimum for initial carve. Production reserved pricing and minimums vary; I'll include options in the pricing sheet.

[19:05] Sam: data-plane specifics: will model weights ever be cached in nodes outside our VPC? If we do VPC peering how does hosted fallback fetch weights?
[19:15] Jared: We serve model weights inside Redwood infra; with VPC peering and private routing the request/response path and model cache stays within region. For hosted fallback we ensure that no plain text payloads are stored beyond configured retention; weights are not stored in your VPC. For Private deployments model weights are fully customer-controlled.

[19:50] Maya: ok good. A bit worried about P95 spikes when multiple clinics start concurrently. Can we pre-warm caches based on schedule?
[19:59] Toni: Yes — managed warmers that run n minutes before schedule. You can also pin top 5k prefixes. We'll work with Beacon to derive which prefixes matter.

[20:30] Jared: Also worth calling out slight transcription issue — in our logs the KV is sometimes labeled "KV cache / K-V chash" in older UI versions; ignore that — new UI normalizes naming.

[21:00] Maya: curious if Redwood has run similar healthcare pilots with on-GPU KV; any references?
[21:07] Alyssa: we have customer-facing case notes (anonymized) — we'll include a short reference list. Not full names due to NDA.

[21:30] Carlos: backup plan if fallback hosted variance is unacceptable: we could pay for higher Dedicated base or do a regional active-active. Thoughts?
[21:40] Jared: Both are valid. Active-active across two Dedicated pools gives strong isolation but increases ops complexity. Increasing base reserved capacity is simpler and keeps caches warm. We'll model cost implications in the pricing sheet.

[22:05] Sam: would be helpful to see stress test graphs for similar mix.
[22:10] Alyssa: we'll attach a bench PDF with graphs.

[22:30] Toni: Quick note on billing granularity: tokens billed per request, but we also surface GPU-runtime metrics so you can correlate cost anomalies to tail events.

[23:00] Maya: any limits on pin list size? We might want to pin a few thousand sessions.
[23:06] Jared: Pin list is configurable but we recommend <10k pinned entries per GPU to avoid memory pressure. For bigger pin lists we use cold backing stores with higher latency.

[23:35] Carlos: operational alerting; can Redwood send alerts when evictions cross threshold?
[23:42] Alyssa: yes, alerts can be wired to PagerDuty or Slack with thresholding.

[24:00] Jared: Real-world gotcha: mixing quant variants across fallback and primary can lead to subtle hallucination differences. Always validate on your clinical eval set. Use Redwood Optimize to automate this.

[24:30] Speaker 6: (background noise)

[24:45] Toni: On the pilot steps: 1) baseline replay run on your infra against hosted and Dedicated simulation; 2) provisioning of Dedicated test pool; 3) VPC peering and KMS keys; 4) run kernel calibration and quant eval; 5) iterate on batching windows. We'll run items 1-3 in parallel.

[25:15] Maya: what data do you need for the replay? Just payloads and arrival times?
[25:22] Jared: payloads, tokenization (we can tokenise for you), arrival timestamps distribution, and historical peak windows. The harness can jitter to simulate noise.

[25:45] Sam: what's the expected work for our infra folks?
[25:50] Toni: open ports for peering, provide a bastion account or ephemeral creds for the bench, and service account for metrics export. We'll provide a runbook.

[26:10] Carlos: encryption at rest — default for hosted?
[26:15] Alyssa: hosted data at rest is encrypted with our keys by default; customer-managed KMS is available for Dedicated and Private. We'll document backup policies.

[26:40] Lena: also include SLA language for audit logs retention and tamper evidence.

[26:47] Alyssa: noted, will include.

[27:00] Jared: Performance tolerance table we propose for the pilot: baseline traffic -> median <120 ms, P95 <450 ms, P99 <900 ms; after warmers and tuning -> median <100 ms, P95 <350 ms. Targets are adjustable to Beacon's clinical needs.

[27:30] Maya: what about canary strategy for rollouts? We want to gradually increase traffic to new kernels.

[27:38] Toni: Redwood Console supports percentage rollouts, mirroring, and automatic rollback on quality/regression monitors. We'll recommend a canary ramp with mirroring first for 5-10% of traffic.

[28:05] Carlos: how will we measure regression? BLEU-like? We have concept of clinical answer fidelity — we want automated checks plus manual review.

[28:15] Jared: Redwood Optimize supports custom eval suites and can compute per-prompt regression metrics. You can set alerts on top-line regression or specific-case fail counts.

[28:40] Sam: curious — for long-term cost savings do you recommend Dedicated only, or hybrid?

[28:46] Alyssa: Hybrid often wins: Dedicated for steady base and hot workloads, hosted for unpredictable bursts. That minimizes cost and keeps tail predictable via warmers and careful overflow policies.

[29:10] Maya: any legal blockers for PHI in hosted?

[29:16] Lena: internal comment — depends on jurisdiction and BAAs. We'll need answers from legal; but architecture constraints from infra perspective are clear: prefer Dedicated/Private for PHI.

[29:35] Alyssa: We'll gather legal-facing docs too.

[30:00] Jared: bench constraints detail: to simulate noisy neighbor you can add background synthetic traffic at X% and observe eviction/hit ratio impact. We'll provide a script that runs background load.

[30:25] Carlos: what about burst billing — if we overflow to hosted will the cost be hidden by Redwood?

[30:30] Alyssa: No — overflow to hosted is billed as hosted usage; we can show cost caps and alerts. For enterprise contracts we can negotiate committed burst blocks.

[30:50] Toni: one more note — we can enforce model variants per route so Hosted fallback doesn't pull an incompatible model. Version pinning is available.

[31:10] Maya: perfect. Any gotchas about sampling randomness producing different outputs across quant variants?

[31:18] Jared: sampling is a separate knob; set seeds for reproducibility in tests. But in prod seeding for all requests is not always feasible. Use eval harness for determinism checks.

[31:45] Speaker 6: (muffled)

[32:00] Alyssa: Quick recap and concrete next steps?
[32:05] Carlos: we want the security pack, pricing, and bench harness. We'll schedule pilot kickoff next week if dates align.
[32:12] Alyssa: noted — action items captured. Jared will own the harness, I'll own pricing and security docs, Toni will coordinate VPC steps.

[32:40] Jared: One last technical tip — prefer per-prompt caching keys that include semantic fingerprint rather than raw text to avoid cache pollution from minor edits. It helps eviction and hit-rate.

[33:10] Sam: interesting. We'll send a sample of our prompt variants.

[33:25] Maya: any reason we shouldn't do a small Dedicated pilot now and add Private later?
[33:30] Alyssa: No — Dedicated is often the natural intermediate step. Private tends to take longer for network and ops approvals.

[33:50] Carlos: procurement question again — can we start with monthly commit for pilot?

[33:56] Alyssa: Yes, pilot-friendly terms exist. We'll include.

[34:15] Toni: ops note: if Beacon wants to pin VIP sessions we should also add health checks to detect single-node issues. We'll share patterns.

[34:40] Maya: any questions we haven't covered re: KV cache behaviour?

[34:47] Jared: only that we'll tune TTL per workload — short TTL for ephemeral chats, longer for session-heavy clinical notes. We'll recommend starting TTL 30 min and iterate.

[35:10] Carlos: ok. Sounds good.

[35:30] Alyssa: We'll queue the next meeting as pilot kickoff tentatively for 2025-11-13. Is that okay?
[35:36] Maya: yes.

[35:50] Speaker 6: (audio)

[36:00] Jared: I'll attach a sample bench output from a previous non-healthcare customer (anonymized) to illustrate variance curves.

[36:20] Toni: Also adding a quick config sample in the email so you can see routing json and warmers example.

[36:34] Maya: great. Regarding metrics retention — how long do logs stay in Console?

[36:40] Alyssa: default 90 days, can be extended as enterprise add-on. We'll include options.

[36:58] Lena: add low-level syslog export requirement for our SIEM.

[37:05] Alyssa: noted. We'll include sample syslog messages.

[37:30] Carlos: is there any place we can test kernel calibration without spinning the full Dedicated pool?

[37:36] Jared: Yes, we have a calibration sandbox that runs on cloud infra; we can calibrate kernels for your prompts with small runs before commit. That reduces risk.

[38:00] Sam: what about model rollbacks mid-day if a kernel regresses?

[38:07] Toni: automatic rollback on quality regression is supported; we can set thresholds to revert to previous variant.

[38:30] Maya: can the console show the per-route rollback history?
[38:35] Alyssa: yes, it shows deployment history, weights, and canary metrics.

[38:50] Jared: small note on replication and failover: if you use on-GPU KV + regional store, design for worst-case 100-150 ms added latency for a single miss during a regional outage.

[39:10] Carlos: acceptable if it's rare.

[39:20] Sam: any legal or export controls on quantized weights?

[39:27] Alyssa: not typically, but we'll confirm.

[39:40] Toni: okay I think we've covered the technical scope.

[39:50] Maya: very helpful. We'll review the pack when you send.

[40:00] Alyssa: action items recap: security pack and pricing (Alyssa), bench harness & scripts (Jared), VPC runbook & ports (Toni), Beacon to provide sample payloads + peak window traces (Maya/Sam), compliance questions (Lena).

[40:30] Carlos: thanks all.

[40:40] Speaker 6: (crosstalk)

[41:00] Alyssa: we'll aim to send materials by Friday. Any quick blockers?

[41:10] Maya: none. 

[41:20] Carlos: good. Looking forward.

[41:30] Jared: I'll follow up with the harness repo link and example commands.

[41:40] Toni: And I'll open the pilot kickoff invite.

[41:50] Lena: thanks.

[42:00] Alyssa: Thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.

Notes (auto): there were intermittent audio glitches, speaker 6 captured some background noise; some transcription tokens mis-labeled KV as "K-V chash" in earlier UI reference — ignore. Several mentions of fallback cost, quantization tradeoffs, and pre-warmers. Links shared post-call: internal bench harness repo (link in email), security pack (link in email), sample pricing sheet (link in email).

Action items (as recorded above): Alyssa to send security pack & pricing; Jared to prepare bench harness and sample runs; Toni to coordinate networking/VPC; Beacon to provide sample payloads and peak traces.

End of transcript.
